<div class="article-top"><a class="back-link" href="../research.html">← Research</a><p class="eyebrow">Aging · Care · Markets</p><h1>Governing Aging Futures</h1><p class="status-line">Research in development</p></div>

::: {.article-copy}

How does population aging become a future that can be forecast, invested in, and addressed through technology?

This research examines the historical formation of aging as a problem of care, economic value, and technological intervention. A working study of the “silver economy” traces changes in policy language and asks how responsibility is assigned among states, markets, families, and individuals.

A related strand follows the making of AI companionship as a response to care needs. Product categories, investment narratives, and ideas of filial obligation bring different expectations of the older person into view: a family member, a care recipient, a consumer, or a user.

The project asks how these expectations become credible and actionable. How does a care need become a market opportunity? How do forecasts and funding decisions shape what gets built? What forms of care become easier—or harder—to recognize within those arrangements?

Historical and conceptual inquiry frames these questions, while a developing ethnographic approach follows how they are negotiated in everyday decisions. My earlier product experience informs the research design; its use as research evidence requires attention to context and consent.

**Status:** working study and research design in development.

:::
